title: Japanese verb tenses
summary: Japanese has two tenses, non-past and past. "Is doing" is a white engine, て + いる, and time words follow a simple に rule.

blocks.text: So far every verb has been in its plain dictionary form. Japanese has just **two tenses**: the **non-past** (the dictionary form) and the **past**. There is no separate present and no separate future.
The non-past is not a present tense
Think of the non-past like English "I eat at six": it covers habits, facts, and above all **things that will happen**. So 犬が食べる most naturally means "The dog will eat."

blocks.en: The dog will eat. (or: The dog eats.)

blocks.text: The past (the **た-form**) is made by changing the end of the verb. For verbs like 食べる and 見る it is simple: **drop る and add た** (食べる → 食べた). Most other verbs change their last kana in a few fixed ways: 飲む → 飲んだ, 行く → 行った. Lesson 5 gives the full recipe. For now, get to know the common verbs in the table.
The third column, the **て-form**, looks just like the past with **て** instead of **た** (飲んだ, 飲んで). You need it for the next part.

For something happening **right now**, Japanese uses **いる**, the "to be" for people and animals, together with the **て-form** of the verb. 食べて is a **white engine**: a verb that cannot pull the train alone but adds information to the real engine, いる. (The table above shows the て-form of common verbs.)
犬が食べている。 The dog is eating.

A **relative** time word (relative to now: 明日 tomorrow, 今日 today, 昨日 yesterday) goes at the start of the sentence with **no particle**. An **absolute** time (a day of the week, a clock time) takes **に**. A good rule of thumb: if English would say "on / at / in", Japanese uses に.

blocks.jp: 明日（私が）ケーキを食べる。

items: Two tenses only: **non-past** (dictionary form) and **past** (**た**: 食べる → 食べた, 飲む → 飲んだ).
The non-past usually points to the **future** or to a habit.
**て + いる** says an action is **in progress**.
Relative time (明日, 今日): **no particle**. Absolute time (火曜日, 六時): **に**.
